title: The Silk Road
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: The Silk Road was not a single road but a vast network of trading routes which linked China with the Mediterranean for about fifteen hundred years. The name was invented in 1877 by a German geographer, Ferdinand von Richthofen, who chose it because silk was the most famous product carried along the way, though traders also carried spices, glass, horses, paper and precious stones. The routes crossed deserts, mountains and some of the harshest country in the world, and few merchants travelled the whole distance. Instead, goods were passed from trader to trader, becoming more expensive at every stage, so that a piece of silk bought in China cost a fortune by the time it reached Rome.

The network began to take shape in the second century before our era, when the Chinese emperor sent an envoy, Zhang Qian, to look for allies against the nomads of the north. His journey took him through Central Asia, and when he returned after more than a decade he brought news of rich cities and fine horses. The emperor was impressed and sent more expeditions. Soon, caravans of camels were carrying silk westwards, and in return came horses, glass and gold. For the Chinese, the trade was valuable not only for the goods but also for the strength it gave the empire along its western border.

Between East and West, a chain of great cities grew rich on the trade. Samarkand and Bukhara, in what is now Uzbekistan, were among the most famous. Their markets sold goods from every corner of the known world, and their craftsmen produced fine cloth, ceramics and paper. Merchants rested in caravanserais, large inns with walled courtyards, where animals could be fed and goods stored safely behind locked gates. A traveller in Samarkand might hear a dozen languages in a single day, and the city was famous as a meeting place of religions and cultures, including Buddhists, Christians, Muslims and Zoroastrians.

The routes carried far more than goods. Ideas, religions and inventions travelled with the caravans. Buddhism spread from India into China along the Silk Road, and Islam later moved eastward into Central Asia. The Chinese invention of papermaking reached the Islamic world in the eighth century, and from there passed on to Europe, where it later made the printing of books affordable. Knowledge of astronomy, mathematics and medicine also passed in both directions, so that scholars in Baghdad, Samarkand and Beijing built on one another's discoveries. Historians often say that the Silk Road was the first great network for the exchange of knowledge.

The routes became safer in the thirteenth century, when the Mongol Empire controlled most of Asia and guarded the roads. In this period the Venetian merchant Marco Polo travelled to China and spent many years at the court of the emperor. When he returned to Europe, he wrote a famous account of what he had seen, which astonished readers with its descriptions of wealthy cities, paper money and a postal system. Some scholars doubt that he saw everything he described, but his book encouraged many Europeans to dream of the East, and it was read by explorers for centuries.

The Silk Road also carried dangers. In the fourteenth century, a terrible disease, the Black Death, is thought to have travelled westward along the trade routes and killed millions of people in Asia and Europe. At the same time, the Mongol Empire weakened, and the roads became less safe again. Meanwhile, European sailors found new sea routes to Asia, which were cheaper and could carry far more cargo than a caravan of camels. By the sixteenth century, most of the long-distance trade had moved to the sea, and many of the cities along the old routes lost their wealth.

Today, the Silk Road is remembered with pride. Dr Aziza Karimova, a historian of Central Asia, says that the great cities along the route developed a culture of tolerance and curiosity, because their prosperity depended on welcoming strangers. Many of the old monuments of Samarkand and Bukhara are now protected, and thousands of tourists visit them every year. Several governments have also announced plans to build new roads, railways and ports along the ancient routes, in what they call a revival of the Silk Road. Historians are cautious, however: they point out that the old network worked because it served the interests of many different peoples.
